title: HyperDoc - procurement/legal: Dedicated throughput SLO language + credits
next_steps: Redwood (Sofia) to send revised Dedicated Throughput SLO language with explicit exclusions + claim process by EOD Thu 2025-03-20
HyperDoc (Daniel/Megan) to return redlines on credits/remedies section and ask for any “most favored customer” clause constraints
Redwood (Lauren/Markus) to share a one-pager explaining how throughput is measured (tokens/sec, windowing, what is counted for streaming) and a sample dashboard screenshot
Schedule a 30-min technical follow-up to confirm committed model/version + context length assumptions for the order form
action_items: Sofia Mendes - Draft contract-ready SLO clause + remedies schedule (include cap, eligibility, notice/claim window) - Due 2025-03-20
Lauren Bishop - Provide customer-facing definition of 'Committed Throughput' and 'Burst' and confirm which tier includes written commitment - Due 2025-03-20
Markus Klein - Send measurement notes on streaming token accounting + what happens during warm pool / cold start - Due 2025-03-21
Megan Liu - Confirm preferred invoicing entity and whether credits must be automatic vs claim-based - Due 2025-03-21
summary: HyperDoc procurement/legal reviewed Redwood Dedicated throughput guarantee language and asked for tighter wording: explicit tokens/sec floor, shorter measurement window, fewer exclusions, and more automatic credits. Redwood aligned on using a defined 'Committed Throughput' measured at the deployment boundary over rolling windows (not per-request), with exclusions for customer-side throttling/misuse, unsupported model changes, and planned maintenance. Remedies discussed: service credits tied to sustained breach, capped, and claim-based with required data. HyperDoc also pushed on failover/HA commitments; Redwood positioned tiering (Premium) for stronger failover posture.
topics: 1) What throughput is guaranteed (tokens/sec vs requests/sec, per deployment vs per route) 2) Measurement window + how streaming tokens are counted 3) Exclusions: customer throttles, model/version changes, prompt/context misuse, maintenance, warm-up 4) Remedies/credits: trigger, cap, claim workflow, evidentiary requirements 5) Failover language and what is included by tier
questions: HyperDoc: Can we define the SLO as p95 tokens/sec per minute? Redwood: we guarantee a floor over a rolling window at the deployment boundary; per-minute p95 is noisy and gameable. HyperDoc: If we see lower throughput, do credits apply automatically? Redwood: credits apply when a sustained breach is confirmed and excludes customer-side throttling; we can discuss a streamlined claim process. HyperDoc: Can we remove the 'supported model list' limitation? Redwood: the guarantee is tied to the committed model/version in the order form to avoid uncontrolled perf variance.
body:
Fireflies.ai transcript

Meeting: HyperDoc - procurement/legal: Dedicated throughput SLO language + credits
Date/Time: Mar 18, 2025 4:02 PM - 4:54 PM (PT)
Duration: 52 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Stephanie Nguyen (Sales), Sofia Mendes (Commercial Counsel), Lauren Bishop (Product - Dedicated), Markus Klein (Solutions)
HyperDoc: Megan Liu (Procurement), Daniel Roth (Legal), Priya Shah (Engineering), Chris Alvarez (Finance)

---

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to go through the throughput SLO language for Dedicated and your redlines on exclusions and remedies. Sofia from our side is here for legal, Lauren for product, and Markus can answer any measurement questions.

[00:18] Megan Liu: Yep. Appreciate it. We’re close but, like, we need the guarantee to be something we can actually point to internally. Our legal team doesn’t love “commercially reasonable efforts” kind of wording.

[00:29] Daniel Roth: And our finance team wants clarity on credits. If the SLO is missed, what happens, when, and how we compute it.

[00:36] Lauren Bishop: Totally. We want it to be concrete and measurable, but also not create weird edge cases where the platform is doing the right thing but we still “breach” on paper.

[00:45] Priya Shah: I’m mainly here to make sure the metric is sane. We’re seeing different token rates depending on prompt length, streaming, tool calls. So we need the definition to match reality.

[01:00] Sofia Mendes: Great. Maybe I’ll start by reading the current proposed clause at a high level, then we can go line-by-line where you have edits.

[01:10] Daniel Roth: Works.

[01:12] Sofia Mendes: The current draft says: Redwood will provide a Dedicated deployment with a “Committed Throughput” of X tokens per second for the “Committed Model” in the “Committed Region,” measured at the Redwood API boundary, averaged over a rolling 15-minute window during the calendar month, excluding scheduled maintenance and customer-caused conditions.

[01:36] Daniel Roth: Right. Our issue: the 15-minute window feels long. If we have a 7-minute drop, that’s still painful for our customers.

[01:45] Megan Liu: And the exclusion list is… it’s a lot. “Customer-caused conditions” is broad.

[01:52] Lauren Bishop: Yeah. We can tighten “customer-caused” to explicit items. The 15-minute window is there because instantaneous tokens/sec is very spiky due to batching and scheduling. But we can talk about alternate windowing.

[02:07] Priya Shah: Can we do something like a one-minute window and then require, say, 95% of minutes in the month meet the threshold? That’s how we do some of our internal SLOs.

[02:20] Markus Klein: We tested that internally. The problem is tokens/sec over one minute gets distorted by a few things: (1) a small number of large-context requests, (2) streaming token accounting, (3) warmup events after scale up. It makes the metric not stable across workloads, and you can end up “failing” even when end-to-end service is fine.

[02:41] Priya Shah: But our users care about those dips.

[02:44] Lauren Bishop: Totally, but we need a contract metric that is attributable and can’t be gamed. For example, a customer can send one massive request with a 120k context, then claim the “tokens per second per minute” dipped, even though that request is outside recommended parameters.

[03:02] Daniel Roth: That’s fair, but we can limit it by defining the workload assumptions in the order form.

[03:08] Sofia Mendes: We can do that, yes—tie the guarantee to a committed model and max context. In fact we prefer that. It’s basically: “Committed Model + max context + streaming mode.” Then we can measure consistently.

[03:23] Megan Liu: Okay. But still, why 15 minutes? Could it be 5?

[03:28] Markus Klein: Five is probably workable. Fifteen is what SRE is comfortable with for noise reduction. But if we specify “rolling 5-minute average” and clarify how we treat warmup, I think it can be okay.

[03:40] Lauren Bishop: I’m open to 5 minutes if we keep the rest of the guardrails.

[03:45] Daniel Roth: So: rolling 5-minute average, then what is the compliance period? Monthly?

[03:50] Sofia Mendes: Usually monthly, yes. The draft is “during each calendar month.” We also track it daily internally but the remedy is monthly.

[04:00] Chris Alvarez: For credits, monthly is okay, but we need to understand if a single bad day triggers credits or if it has to be sustained.

[04:09] Sofia Mendes: In the current draft, credits trigger if the service is below the committed throughput for more than a defined percentage of eligible time in the month.

[04:18] Megan Liu: Eligible time meaning after exclusions.

[04:20] Sofia Mendes: Correct.

[04:22] Daniel Roth: Let’s talk metric definition first, then exclusions, then remedies.

[04:27] Sofia Mendes: Okay.

[04:28] Daniel Roth: We want the metric to be unambiguous: is it tokens generated, tokens accepted, or tokens billed? And does it count prompt tokens? Because some providers count prompt + completion. Some only completion.

[04:41] Markus Klein: Great question. For throughput, we define “output tokens/sec” at the inference boundary, i.e., generated tokens. Prompt tokens are part of latency but not part of output rate. We can add an explicit definition: numerator is model output tokens successfully produced; denominator is time in seconds over the window.

[04:59] Priya Shah: And for streaming? We stream tokens. Are you counting them as they stream or when the request ends?

[05:05] Markus Klein: We count them as they are emitted. There was a bug earlier this quarter where streaming got double-counted in a metric export—fixed now. But contract-wise we can define it as emitted tokens.

[05:18] Priya Shah: Good.

[05:20] Daniel Roth: Where is it measured? You say “Redwood API boundary.” We need that to exclude our own network. But if there’s internal Redwood routing between regions, does that count as your boundary or not?

[05:33] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, requests terminate in the region of the deployment. The “boundary” is effectively our ingress for that deployment. If we do an internal failover (which is tier-dependent), that’s still within Redwood responsibility. But we should be precise: measured at the deployment ingress, tagged by deployment ID.

[05:51] Sofia Mendes: I’ll update wording to “measured at Redwood’s deployment ingress for the Dedicated Deployment (deployment_id), excluding customer network and client-side time.”

[06:02] Megan Liu: That’s helpful.

[06:04] Daniel Roth: Next: “Committed Model.” Our redline was to remove the restriction to specific model versions because you might upgrade models.

[06:12] Lauren Bishop: Right, but model upgrades change performance. Tokens/sec can shift materially across versions, quantization profiles, etc. The guarantee needs a pinned model version. We can offer a process: if you want to upgrade, we benchmark and then amend the order form or update the committed throughput.

[06:30] Priya Shah: Could we say “Committed Model family” like Llama-3.1-70B and then any patch versions within that?

[06:36] Markus Klein: Maybe. The thing that bites is not just “patch versions,” it’s different runtime settings, context lengths, or tool calling settings. But we can allow “minor version updates that Redwood designates as performance-equivalent” or something like that.

[06:53] Sofia Mendes: Contract language could be: “Committed Model means the model and version identified in the Order Form, or a successor version designated by Redwood as substantially equivalent for throughput.” That gives you an upgrade path without reopening the whole SLO every time.

[07:08] Daniel Roth: That’s better.

[07:10] Megan Liu: As long as it’s not unilateral. Like you can’t just declare something equivalent and it’s worse.

[07:15] Sofia Mendes: Understood. We can also say “designated in writing” and you have the right to reject if it materially reduces throughput. We’ll propose balanced language.

[07:27] Stephanie Nguyen: On the commercial side, we’d still recommend formalizing upgrades because you’ll likely want quality checks too.

[07:34] Priya Shah: Yep.

[07:36] Daniel Roth: Okay. Exclusions. Your list includes “customer-side throttling.” Explain what you mean.

[07:42] Markus Klein: If your client is limiting concurrency (like you send 2 requests at a time) you might not be able to reach the committed throughput. The deployment can do, say, 3k tokens/sec, but if you only feed it one request at a time with long think times between, observed throughput is low. That’s not a Redwood performance issue.

[08:03] Priya Shah: That makes sense. But how do you detect that?

[08:06] Markus Klein: We see incoming request rate, concurrency, queue depth. If queue is empty a lot, you’re not driving enough load to saturate committed throughput.

[08:16] Daniel Roth: So is there a minimum load requirement to test the SLO?

[08:20] Lauren Bishop: Yes. The SLO is evaluated when the deployment is “eligible,” meaning it has sufficient offered load. Otherwise it’s not meaningful. We can define eligibility: e.g., average queue depth above a threshold or concurrency above N for at least X% of the window.

[08:38] Megan Liu: We don’t want a definition where it’s always “ineligible.”

[08:42] Lauren Bishop: Totally. That’s why we need something simple like: eligible if offered load >= committed throughput demand. In practice we can phrase it as: eligible when your requests are not rate-limited by you and not idle.

[08:55] Sofia Mendes: For the contract, we should keep it readable. Something like: “SLO applies during periods when Customer is submitting sufficient requests such that the Dedicated Deployment is not idle and is not constrained by Customer-side rate limits.” Then we can reference an engineering appendix for exact signals.

[09:12] Daniel Roth: Okay.

[09:14] Daniel Roth: Next exclusion: “unsupported models or configuration.” We asked to narrow.

[09:20] Sofia Mendes: We can specify: excluded if Customer uses a model other than the Committed Model, or exceeds Committed max context, or uses unsupported parameters. That’s more concrete than “unsupported configuration.”

[09:34] Priya Shah: Include “context length.” That’s the big one.

[09:36] Markus Klein: Yep. Because long context shifts compute from decode to prefill and throughput looks different.

[09:45] Megan Liu: You also have “abuse or misuse patterns.” That’s subjective.

[09:49] Lauren Bishop: We can remove subjective language. Replace with explicit misuse conditions: sustained 5xx due to invalid requests, repeated timeouts due to exceeding max tokens, that kind of thing.

[10:04] Daniel Roth: Better.

[10:06] Sofia Mendes: Planned maintenance is another. Our standard is: scheduled maintenance with 72-hour notice, and it is excluded from SLO measurement for that duration.

[10:17] Megan Liu: We asked for 7 days notice.

[10:20] Sofia Mendes: For Dedicated we can usually do 7 days, but some security patches are shorter. Can we do: “at least 7 days when practicable, and no less than 72 hours except for emergency maintenance”?

[10:33] Daniel Roth: That’s fine.

[10:36] Chris Alvarez: Emergency maintenance—does that include outages? Like you just call it emergency and it’s excluded.

[10:42] Sofia Mendes: Not outages. Emergency maintenance is typically security patching to prevent a known exploit. Outages are not excluded.

[10:50] Lauren Bishop: And we can cap emergency maintenance exclusions, like reasonable limits.

[10:57] Daniel Roth: Another thing: “warm pool behavior.” Your language excludes “warm-up periods after scale events.” We don’t like that.

[11:06] Lauren Bishop: To be clear, Dedicated capacity is reserved. There shouldn’t be frequent cold starts. But if you have burst autoscaling, new nodes might take a few minutes to warm up. We’d rather not have that counted as a breach.

[11:22] Priya Shah: But if it’s Dedicated, why are we warming up at all? Shouldn’t you keep it hot?

[11:28] Markus Klein: Depends on tier. Premium keeps a warm pool and spare capacity, Standard is more cost optimized. If you buy a committed baseline with burst, the burst pool may not be pre-warmed at the same level.

[11:42] Megan Liu: We’re looking at Plus or Premium. We want predictable.

[11:46] Stephanie Nguyen: You were leaning Plus in the last call, but if failover and warm pool guarantees are important, Premium may be the cleanest path.

[11:55] Daniel Roth: Let’s stay on the language. If we go Premium, can you remove warm-up exclusion?

[12:02] Lauren Bishop: We can narrow it. For Premium, we can say: warm pool is maintained such that scale-up warmup does not materially reduce throughput below committed floor for more than, say, a short stabilization window.

[12:17] Sofia Mendes: Contractually, we can define a small “stabilization period” exclusion—like first 2 minutes after a capacity add event—rather than a broad exclusion.

[12:27] Priya Shah: That’s reasonable.

[12:30] Daniel Roth: Remedies and credits. Our proposal: if throughput is below committed for any rolling 5-minute window, you provide credits automatically.

[12:40] Sofia Mendes: We can’t do “any window” because of noise and because credits would be triggered by brief blips that don’t reflect sustained service failure. Industry standard is a monthly availability or performance percentage.

[12:54] Megan Liu: But this is a throughput guarantee. If we can’t serve, we churn users.

[12:58] Lauren Bishop: Understood. We can tighten triggers without making it per-window. Example: if during eligible time in a month, we are below committed throughput for more than 1% of eligible minutes, credits apply. The window is still 5 minutes, but you aggregate breaches.

[13:17] Daniel Roth: Okay. Then the credit schedule—your draft says “up to 10% of monthly fees.” We asked for higher.

[13:25] Chris Alvarez: Specifically, we asked for 25% if you miss by more than 5% over the month.

[13:31] Sofia Mendes: We can discuss, but we usually cap at 10% for performance SLOs. For availability we sometimes go higher. Throughput is influenced by workload.

[13:44] Priya Shah: If workload is within committed assumptions, that’s on you.

[13:48] Sofia Mendes: Right, but measurement and attribution are still tricky. The cap is also to keep remedies proportional.

[13:56] Daniel Roth: Our internal procurement policy expects meaningful remedies for “material breach.”

[14:02] Sofia Mendes: We can add: if there’s repeated breaches, you can terminate for cause or have an additional remedy. Credits are one piece.

[14:10] Megan Liu: Termination language helps, but we still want a bigger credit.

[14:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Would it help if we structure it in tiers? Like 5% credit for minor miss, 10% for larger, plus optional incident support commitments.

[14:25] Chris Alvarez: Maybe.

[14:27] Sofia Mendes: Proposed structure: If Committed Throughput is not met for more than 1% of eligible time in a month: 5% credit. If more than 2.5%: 10% credit. Cap at 10%.

[14:42] Daniel Roth: That’s still capped.

[14:44] Sofia Mendes: Another lever is to define “service credit against next invoice” plus “dedicated escalation / premium support response” obligations. But yes, our standard cap is 10.

[14:55] Megan Liu: Our last vendor, Together, offered 20% cap.

[14:59] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. Dedicated with reserved GPUs is a bit different model, but we can take that back internally.

[15:07] Lauren Bishop: We can also talk about operational mitigations—like adding headroom, failover, warm pool—those reduce the chance you ever need credits.

[15:18] Priya Shah: We still want the paper guarantee.

[15:21] Sofia Mendes: Of course.

[15:22] Daniel Roth: Another legal point: claim process. Your draft requires notice within 10 days and “reasonable evidence.” We asked to remove the evidence requirement.

[15:34] Sofia Mendes: We need some evidence so we can validate it’s eligible time and not customer throttling. But we can simplify: you notify us via support ticket referencing the deployment ID and time range, and we will verify using our logs. You shouldn’t have to provide extensive data.

[15:51] Megan Liu: So we file a ticket, you confirm using your dashboards.

[15:54] Sofia Mendes: Exactly.

[15:56] Priya Shah: Could the dashboard be visible to us? Like SLO status.

[16:00] Markus Klein: Yes. In the console we have a throughput floor panel for Dedicated. It shows observed tokens/sec vs committed, eligible time, and recent breaches. We can share screenshots and enable it for your org.

[16:14] Priya Shah: That helps because we can self-diagnose.

[16:16] Daniel Roth: Great. Then you can keep an evidence requirement as long as it’s just “deployment ID + time range.”

[16:23] Sofia Mendes: Agreed.

[16:25] Chris Alvarez: Also: are credits applied automatically once you detect breach, or only on claim?

[16:32] Sofia Mendes: Standard is claim-based, but we can commit to responding within a defined time and confirming eligibility. For Premium tier, we can potentially do proactive notification.

[16:45] Megan Liu: We prefer automatic.

[16:47] Sofia Mendes: We can’t commit to fully automatic credits because we must verify exclusions. But we can make it low-friction.

[16:55] Stephanie Nguyen: In practice, when there’s an incident, we already open an internal incident and notify customers. The claim is more of a formal step.

[17:05] Daniel Roth: Okay.

[17:06] Daniel Roth: Failover. Your SLO language says nothing about regional failover. We asked to add: if throughput in region drops, you failover to another region.

[17:16] Lauren Bishop: That depends on tier and on whether your workload can tolerate cross-region latency and data residency constraints. We can provide HA within a region (multi-node, redundancy) and, for Premium, an optional secondary region warm standby.

[17:33] Priya Shah: We can tolerate us-west to us-east in worst case. Not ideal but better than down.

[17:39] Megan Liu: Our security team will ask about data residency; but for us it’s US-only.

[17:44] Sofia Mendes: We can add a separate “Failover” clause: for Premium with multi-region configured, Redwood will use commercially reasonable efforts to fail over within a target time. But be careful—failover is not strictly throughput SLO, it’s incident response.

[18:02] Daniel Roth: Can it be an obligation, not just “reasonable efforts.”

[18:07] Sofia Mendes: We can make it a defined operational commitment if it’s in the tier entitlement. I’d rather put it in the Order Form as a purchased feature: “multi-region failover enabled.”

[18:18] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s consistent with how we package it.

[18:22] Priya Shah: Separate from failover, can you confirm: Dedicated means we are not sharing GPUs.

[18:28] Markus Klein: Correct. Dedicated pool is isolated. Depending on shape, it may be a node group only for you. No other customer traffic on those GPUs.

[18:38] Priya Shah: Good.

[18:40] Daniel Roth: Another small redline: define “tokens.” Some contracts get weird.

[18:45] Sofia Mendes: Yes. We can define “Token means a unit of text as processed by the Committed Model tokenizer.” And we’ll specify “output tokens” for throughput.

[18:56] Megan Liu: Great.

[18:58] Priya Shah: And tool calls? Like function calling. Sometimes the model emits JSON. Tokens are tokens.

[19:03] Markus Klein: Correct. Still output tokens.

[19:06] Daniel Roth: So where are we landing on the measurement window? You said maybe 5 minutes.

[19:11] Lauren Bishop: Tentatively: rolling 5-minute average, evaluated during “eligible time,” aggregated monthly.

[19:19] Daniel Roth: And the committed throughput number—will that be one number or can we have different numbers for different routes?

[19:26] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, we prefer one per deployment for the committed model. If you have multiple routes with different max tokens, it complicates. We can define separate deployments if you need different commitments.

[19:40] Priya Shah: We have chat and summarization. Different lengths.

[19:44] Markus Klein: We can still do one deployment if you accept that the guarantee is an aggregate. But if summarization dominates, it may shift prefill. We should align on workload profile.

[19:56] Stephanie Nguyen: This is why we wanted a sizing follow-up—so we don’t promise the wrong number.

[20:01] Megan Liu: Okay.

[20:03] Daniel Roth: Back to exclusions: You had “third-party outages.” What third party?

[20:08] Sofia Mendes: Cloud provider outages that are outside Redwood control. But for Dedicated we typically can mitigate within a region. Still, if there’s a major cloud event, we may need an exclusion.

[20:22] Daniel Roth: We generally do not accept “cloud provider” as an exclusion.

[20:26] Sofia Mendes: Understood. We can narrow it to: excluded only to the extent the outage is caused by the underlying cloud provider and is verified, and only if it affects the dedicated deployment. But yes, we can try to keep it minimal.

[20:41] Lauren Bishop: And if you buy multi-region, we can reduce impact.

[20:46] Chris Alvarez: This is turning into Premium again.

[20:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Probably, given your requirements.

[20:51] Megan Liu: Let’s assume Premium for now; we can still negotiate.

[20:55] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[20:56] Daniel Roth: Remedies: Do credits apply to the full monthly fees or just the impacted component? You have “affected service.”

[21:04] Sofia Mendes: For Dedicated, it’s typically the monthly Dedicated fee for that deployment (or portion of it) because it’s a reserved resource. We can clarify: credit is percentage of the monthly recurring fee for the impacted Dedicated Deployment.

[21:20] Daniel Roth: Okay.

[21:22] Priya Shah: Can we also require you to provide incident report when there is a breach.

[21:28] Lauren Bishop: Yes. We can commit to a post-incident RCA for Severity 1 incidents. For performance SLO misses that are small, we might not do a full RCA unless requested.

[21:40] Megan Liu: We want at least a written summary.

[21:42] Stephanie Nguyen: We can do that as part of Premium support—incident comms and summaries.

[21:47] Sofia Mendes: Contract: we can say “upon request, Redwood will provide a written summary of material service incidents impacting the SLO.”

[21:58] Daniel Roth: Fine.

[22:00] Daniel Roth: I want to make sure “eligible time” doesn’t let you avoid responsibility by saying we weren’t sending enough traffic. We have variable load. Nights are lower.

[22:10] Markus Klein: If you’re low load, you’re not going to “breach.” The SLO just won’t be evaluated. But you also won’t need throughput at that time. The issue is if you’re low load and still want credits, that wouldn’t make sense.

[22:24] Priya Shah: But we might still see slowdowns at low load due to some background thing.

[22:28] Lauren Bishop: That would show up as latency, not throughput. We can talk about latency SLO separately if needed, but this contract is throughput guarantee.

[22:38] Daniel Roth: Understood.

[22:40] Megan Liu: But procurement still wants one number.

[22:43] Stephanie Nguyen: We can keep it as throughput, and we can add a support response SLA, and we can attach the operational dashboard so it’s transparent.

[22:52] Sofia Mendes: And we can define that Redwood will not materially reduce the dedicated capacity allocated to you below what is needed to meet committed throughput, except as allowed by scheduled maintenance.

[23:05] Daniel Roth: Okay.

[23:07] Sofia Mendes: Let me summarize proposed edits so far:
- Measurement: output tokens/sec, measured at deployment ingress.
- Window: rolling 5-minute average.
- Period: monthly evaluation with % of eligible time.
- Eligible time: when sufficient offered load and not customer-side throttled.
- Committed Model: model+version in Order Form, with “substantially equivalent successor” option.
- Exclusions: scheduled maintenance (notice), emergency maintenance (narrow), customer throttling/idle, exceeding max context/unsupported model, invalid requests.
- Remedies: credit schedule with cap (still under debate), claim process simplified.

[23:45] Megan Liu: That’s right.

[23:47] Daniel Roth: But credit cap is still the big gap.

[23:50] Sofia Mendes: Yes.

[23:51] Chris Alvarez: We need something we can justify as risk coverage.

[23:56] Stephanie Nguyen: If we move you to Premium, there’s more built-in redundancy and we can also offer stronger support SLAs. Sometimes customers accept a lower credit cap with stronger operational commitments.

[24:09] Megan Liu: Potentially.

[24:11] Daniel Roth: What support SLA do you propose?

[24:14] Stephanie Nguyen: Premium: 24/7 on-call escalation, initial response 15 minutes for Sev 1, ongoing updates every 30 minutes until mitigated.

[24:24] Sofia Mendes: That would be in a support exhibit rather than the throughput clause.

[24:28] Daniel Roth: Okay.

[24:30] Priya Shah: Can we discuss the “gaming” concern? You mentioned “one massive request.” If we define maximum context length and maximum output tokens, doesn’t that address it?

[24:40] Markus Klein: Mostly yes. But there’s still workload mix. E.g., many short requests vs a few long ones. Throughput in tokens/sec should still be consistent if you’re saturating decode, but prefill-heavy workloads can reduce decode rate. If we commit to a tokens/sec floor, we need to ensure we’re not committing to an impossible number for your mix.

[25:02] Priya Shah: So we should specify workload assumptions.

[25:05] Lauren Bishop: Exactly. That’s why we want a sizing appendix: typical input length distribution, typical output length distribution, streaming on/off.

[25:14] Daniel Roth: Legal doesn’t want a huge appendix.

[25:17] Sofia Mendes: We can keep it light: “Committed max context = N tokens; max output = M tokens; streaming enabled; tool calling enabled.” That’s probably sufficient.

[25:28] Megan Liu: Fine.

[25:30] Chris Alvarez: One more finance question: if we exceed committed throughput (burst), is that billed separately? And does that affect SLO measurement?

[25:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Burst is optional and metered separately if you exceed baseline. SLO measurement is for committed baseline; burst is best-effort unless explicitly included.

[25:50] Megan Liu: Then the contract should say burst is excluded from SLO.

[25:53] Sofia Mendes: Yes—good point. We’ll define “Committed Throughput” vs “Burst Capacity” and clarify that burst does not increase the committed floor unless purchased.

[26:05] Priya Shah: But if you shed our burst traffic, that’s okay.

[26:08] Lauren Bishop: Right.

[26:10] Daniel Roth: Okay. But we still want the SLO to apply to baseline even if we’re bursting.

[26:15] Markus Klein: It does. We have admission control that protects the baseline. Bursts can be queued or shed first.

[26:23] Priya Shah: Good.

[26:25] Daniel Roth: Another redline: You had “sole and exclusive remedy.” We struck that.

[26:30] Sofia Mendes: We can’t fully remove it; credits are typically sole remedy for SLO violations. But you can still have termination for uncured material breach as a general remedy. We can craft it so that credits are the remedy for the specific SLO miss, but not limiting other rights for other breaches.

[26:50] Daniel Roth: That’s what we want.

[26:53] Sofia Mendes: Okay.

[26:54] Megan Liu: Timeline: We need to finalize by end of month for procurement committee.

[26:59] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood.

[27:01] Sofia Mendes: I can turn around a revised clause by Thursday with the narrowed exclusions and the 5-minute window. Credit cap we may need internal approval if we go above 10.

[27:12] Chris Alvarez: Can you at least propose an option? Like 10% standard, 20% for Premium.

[27:18] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s a reasonable package to propose.

[27:20] Lauren Bishop: Premium already costs more because we reserve headroom; higher credits might be acceptable. But we need finance sign-off.

[27:27] Sofia Mendes: I’ll propose two options and we can align.
